question: What is the primary focus of epidemiology in community health nursing?

options.A: Studying disease patterns in entire populations
options.B: Managing financial budgets for local health clinics
options.C: Diagnosing rare diseases in hospital laboratories
options.D: Providing bedside nursing care to individual patients

explanation: Epidemiology focuses on tracking diseases and health events across whole groups rather than single individuals. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why is epidemiologic data vital for community health nurses?

options.A: It eliminates the need for physical examinations in clinics
options.B: It replaces the need to interview sick community members
options.C: It guarantees that funding will increase every fiscal year
options.D: It helps plan effective prevention and allocate resources wisely

explanation: Having accurate data allows nurses to target interventions where they are needed most to protect the community. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is an example of secondary epidemiologic data?

options.A: Measuring the mid-upper arm circumference of children
options.B: Interviewing village elders about local health beliefs
options.C: Conducting blood pressure checks at a local market square
options.D: Reviewing past mortality records from the health ministry

explanation: Secondary data refers to information that was already gathered by other agencies or researchers in the past. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h2)

question: A community health nurse conducts a household survey to count active tuberculosis cases. What type of data is this primarily?
explanation: Counting active cases involves numerical measurements, which classifies the information as quantitative data. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which data collection method involves talking directly with trusted village leaders about local health issues?
explanation: Key informants are knowledgeable community figures who provide deep insight into local health behaviors and needs. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h3)

question: A nurse wants to assess how community members handle their household drinking water. Which method is most appropriate?

options.D: Direct observation of water storage practices

explanation: Direct observation allows the nurse to see actual daily behaviors regarding water handling rather than relying on reported answers. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h3)

question: What does the term 'reliability' mean in the context of data collection?

options.A: Getting consistent results if the measurement is repeated
options.B: Collecting information quickly during an emergency
options.C: Storing physical records in a secure steel cabinet
options.D: Ensuring the data matches the exact true value

explanation: Reliability refers to the stability and consistency of data collection tools and methods over multiple uses. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a good way to maintain high data quality?

options.A: Relying entirely on memory without writing down field notes
options.B: Training field staff properly before surveys begin
options.C: Conducting routine spot-checks and data audits
options.D: Using clear and pre-tested data collection forms

explanation: Human memory is fallible; failing to record data immediately in the field leads to severe omissions and errors. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of analyzing epidemiologic data?

options.A: To turn raw numbers into understandable patterns of health
options.B: To replace the need for physical patient examinations
options.C: To make collection forms look neat and professional
options.D: To hide mistakes made during community surveys

explanation: Analysis organizes scattered information so nurses can see where and why health issues are occurring. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h5)

question: A nurse compares the number of malaria cases between two villages with different population sizes. Why is calculating a rate better than just looking at raw counts?

options.A: Rates eliminate the need for laboratory confirmations
options.B: Raw counts are always illegal to use in public health
options.C: Rates account for differences in total population size
options.D: Raw counts are harder to write down on paper forms

explanation: Comparing raw counts alone can be misleading if one village is much larger than the other; rates provide a fair comparison. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h5)

question: When is epidemiologic data considered fully utilised in public health?

options.A: When it drives practical action and health interventions
options.B: When it is printed in a foreign medical textbook
options.C: When field logbooks are completely filled with ink
options.D: When it is locked away safely in a government vault

explanation: Data exists to guide decision-making and solve real community health problems, not just sit on a shelf. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h6)

question: A nurse notices from clinic data that adolescent girls in a rural area have low uptake of tetanus vaccinations. What should be the next step based on data utilization principles?

options.A: Ignore the data because teenagers are generally healthy
options.B: Design a targeted outreach campaign to educate and vaccinate the girls
options.C: Stop collecting vaccination data to save time and energy
options.D: Punish the local clinic staff for failing to report high numbers

explanation: The nurse uses the identified gap in data to direct resources and action toward the unprotected group. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h6)

question: What must a nurse obtain from a community member before conducting an individual health interview or examination?
explanation: Every participant has the right to know what a study involves and agree voluntarily before giving personal data. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h7)

question: Why is patient confidentiality especially critical during community health data collection?

options.A: It prevents the government from spending money on printing paper
options.B: It protects personal dignity and maintains community trust in health workers
options.C: It ensures that nurses never have to speak with village leaders
options.D: It makes data analysis much faster for computer software programs

explanation: If people fear their private health details will be exposed, they will hide illnesses and avoid public clinics. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is a common challenge faced when gathering data in rural community settings?

options.A: Cultural suspicions and logistical barriers like bad roads
options.B: An overabundance of trained epidemiologists in every village
options.C: Having too many computers and electricity sources available
options.D: Patients demanding financial payment for answering questions

explanation: Fieldwork often involves poor infrastructure and occasional mistrust from residents who misunderstand health activities. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h8)

question: How can a community health nurse best address local suspicion regarding health surveys?

options.A: Ignore the suspicious residents and only interview hospital staff
options.B: Collect data secretly at night without telling community members
options.C: Involve respected local leaders and explain the purpose clearly
options.D: Threaten residents with fines if they refuse to answer questions

explanation: Partnering with trusted community figures helps dispel myths and reassures residents that the health activities are safe and beneficial. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h8)
